epigraph.author: Executive Dossier Summary

web_blocks.html: McKesson Corporation (NYSE: MCK) runs North America's largest drug distribution toll-road. It generated $403.43 billion in FY2026 revenue and $5.41 billion in Free Cash Flow [2, 19]. The company operates inside a three-player oligopoly that controls over 90% of U.S. drug distribution [19]. On business quality, McKesson earns a clear COMPOUNDER_PASS, PASS_WITH_WATCH KPI health, and a TIER_1 CORE_ALPHA rating [1, 2]. Management is also upgrading the profit pool. It exited lower-margin European retail and separated Medical-Surgical Solutions (Wellverse) with a $1.25 billion Apollo investment [2, 9, 10]. At the same time, it is scaling Oncology & Multispecialty (2.96% adjusted operating margin, +53% YoY) and Prescription Technology Solutions (19.45% margin) [2].

Great businesses still require disciplined entry prices. At the November 20, 2026 close of $1,069.43 (TradingView $1,069.72), MCK trades +9.76% above its rising 50-day SMA ($974.32) [24]. Its weekly RSI sits at an overbought 71.10 inside a confirmed S&P 500 Downtrend (40.4% breadth >50DMA, 10 distribution days in 25d) [24]. Buying at $1,069.43 against our $857.69 structural stop offers only 0.62:1 reward-to-risk to our $1,200.00 base target [24]. Our options desk also flags NO_OPTIONS_EDGE (1.17:1 call spread R:R). Our capital verdict is therefore ACCUMULATE_ON_DIP into the $940.00–$985.00 pullback shelf, where asymmetry flips to 1.69:1.

book_paragraphs: Every institutional dossier should start where a portfolio manager's morning meeting begins. You need the bottom line, the exact price levels, and the reason to deploy cash or wait. For McKesson Corporation as of November 20, 2026, the verdict separates business quality from market timing.

First, look at the business. McKesson passes our fundamental review and earns a COMPOUNDER_PASS verdict with a Tier 1 Core Alpha rating. Think of McKesson as the vital toll road of American medicine. It moves $403.43 billion of drugs and medical supplies a year inside a three-player oligopoly that controls over 90% of U.S. drug distribution [2, 19]. Across ten years of audited cash flow statements, McKesson has never posted a negative operating cash flow year. It generates $4 billion to $6 billion annually while needing less than 0.2% of revenue in capital spending [2, 15]. Even better, McKesson is no longer just a low-margin logistics utility. It exited European retail and is separating its Medical-Surgical Wellverse unit with Apollo's $1.25 billion investment [2, 9, 10]. Management is pouring that focus into Oncology & Multispecialty and Prescription Technology Solutions, lifting the profit mix toward clinical and software services [2].

Honest underwriting also names every risk upfront, so we flag KPI health as PASS_WITH_WATCH. Four items sit on our watch list. First, CVS Health accounts for roughly 24% of revenue, though its contract now runs through June 2032 [2, 5]. Second, $5.06 billion in opioid settlement liabilities remain on the balance sheet through 2038 [2, 21]. Third, redeemable physician minority interests stand at $2.56 billion [3]. Fourth, Medicare Part B negotiation, 340B rebate shifts, and cyber risks require constant tracking [4, 20].

Second, look at the valuation and the tape. At $1,069.43 per share, McKesson trades at 20.38x forward earnings and 16.63x EV/EBITDA [25]. It carries a sector-best 1.33 PEG ratio and a 76.71% return on invested capital [25]. Reverse DCF math shows the market only prices in about 7.8% annual free cash flow growth, or 11.3% EPS growth after buybacks. That sits well below management's +17% to +19% fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS growth guidance of $45.60 to $46.40 [6, 25]. Fundamentally, the stock is not in a bubble. Technically, however, it is stretched. McKesson is a standout Stage 2 leader (+32.04% relative strength over 63 days), but its weekly RSI has hit an overbought 71.10 [24]. Shares also sit nearly 10% above their rising 50-day moving average ($974.32) during an S&P 500 Downtrend [24].

When you combine those two facts, the math makes the decision for us. Buying at $1,069.43 against our $857.69 structural stop risks $211.74 per share for $130.57 of upside to our $1,200.00 base target. That is a weak 0.62:1 reward-to-risk ratio, and our options desk confirms NO_OPTIONS_EDGE. By contrast, waiting for a normal pullback into the $940.00–$985.00 support shelf transforms the setup. It turns the exact same business into a 1.69:1 entry with +20.7% probability-weighted upside. Because we hold zero shares (NOT_HELD), our plan is simple. Keep 100% of earmarked capital in cash, set limit alerts at $940.00–$985.00, and let the Downtrend bring this Tier 1 compounder to our price.

We also checked whether any healthcare substitute deserves our cash right now. Eli Lilly trades at 44.26x trailing earnings with 0.71:1 reward-to-risk at current prices [25]. Cencora trades at 15.63x forward earnings, yet carries 3.06x debt-to-equity and 23.63% ROIC versus McKesson's 76.71% ROIC [25, 26]. Neither peer matches McKesson's mix of oligopoly durability and specialty software growth. Staying 100% in cash preserves dry powder for the clear category leader.

book_subsections.title: How to Use This Ten-Chapter Dossier
paragraphs: Chapters 1 through 6 of this monograph were written completely blind to today's share price and chart. They trace McKesson's path from an 1833 New York apothecary to a $403.43 billion North American healthcare giant [2, 17]. They also break down every segment with real-world examples, map negative working capital, and audit ten years of cash flows [2, 15].

Chapters 7 through 9 bring that fundamental work into the live market of November 20, 2026. We test implied growth with a Reverse DCF and compare McKesson against Cencora, Cardinal Health, and Henry Schein. We also inspect the Stage 2 chart across weekly, daily, and four-hour timeframes. Finally, we stress-test Bull and Bear cases into a clear, no-FOMO action plan. Every number traces back to primary filings and verified market snapshots.

book_subsections.title: The Core Alpha Checklist: Why McKesson Earns Tier 1 Status
paragraphs: Few companies check every box on an institutional Core Alpha checklist, which makes McKesson stand out. First, it owns a physical and regulatory moat that software startups or e-commerce entrants cannot copy. Second, it converts negative working capital and tiny capex into $5.41 billion of annual free cash flow and 76.71% ROIC [2, 25]. Third, management has shown strong capital discipline. Its FY2027E sources-and-uses bridge pairs $1.25 billion in Apollo Wellverse equity, $2.25 billion in Med-Surg separation debt proceeds, and $5.4 billion to $6.0 billion in annual free cash flow—roughly $9.0 billion to $9.5 billion in total sources—to fund the $2.25 billion Precision Medicine Group acquisition (closed November 2, 2026), the $1.40 billion proposed 49% Option Care Health stake, and $4.5 billion to $5.0 billion in annual share buybacks [2, 9, 10, 12, 13]. If needed during integration, buybacks can moderate to $3.5 billion to $4.0 billion to keep net leverage below 1.5x EBITDA.

All that remains is our own execution discipline. Never confuse a great business with a great entry price on an overbought week. Keep your alerts live at $940.00 to $985.00, keep your structural invalidation stop ready at $857.69, and let the market come to you.

book_subsections.title: The Patience Edge in Compounder Investing
paragraphs: Across many institutional case studies, the gap between average returns and elite compounding rarely comes from finding obscure stocks. It comes from refusing to overpay for obvious winners when they stretch above trend. Instead, disciplined investors step in when normal market turbulence delivers those winners to support. McKesson is a textbook example: a $403.43 billion toll-road oligopoly with 76.71% ROIC and +17% to +19% fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS growth [2, 6, 25].

At $1,069.43, the tape asks us to wait. At $940.00 to $985.00, the math invites us to act with conviction. Let's now step back to Chapter 1 and trace how an 1833 New York apothecary built one of the strongest distribution franchises in modern finance.

As you read or listen through the ten chapters ahead, keep our dual verdict in mind. Business quality is a clear COMPOUNDER_PASS, while capital timing is a disciplined ACCUMULATE_ON_DIP. Every segment table, cash-flow waterfall, peer multiple, and technical level points to the same practical conclusion. Own McKesson for the long haul, but let price come to your support shelf first.
That is the standard we hold across every company in our research desk. We put unbiased fundamental underwriting first, strict valuation and technical asymmetry second, and zero tolerance for FOMO.

Whether you are evaluating McKesson as a new position or tracking it on your watchlist, the message is clear. Respect the $403.43 billion toll-road moat and the +32.04% relative strength. Wait patiently for the $940.00–$985.00 buy zone where 1.69:1 asymmetry awaits. Now let's dive into Chapter 1 and trace McKesson's journey from 1833 to today.

Keep this simple scorecard in mind throughout the rest of the book. Our buy zone sits at $940.00 to $985.00, with a hard structural stop-loss at $857.69 below the 30-week and 200-day moving averages. Our base-case fair value target is $1,200.00 ($1,350.00 bull, $820.00 bear). Meanwhile, 100% of our earmarked capital stays in cash until the Downtrend market delivers McKesson to support.
